# Shockley, the Eight, and the Spinoff {#sec-4-02}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1956–1960
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** What happens when a genius cannot manage people?

**The answer.** His company fails and his industry is born. Shockley brought the
best semiconductor minds in the world to Mountain View in 1956 and drove eight
of them out within eighteen months, and those eight founded Fairchild. The
Valley's reproductive mechanism is not invention. It is the spinoff — talent
exiting bad leadership, taking the knowledge, and starting again nearby.

**The mechanism.** Elite network reproduction, running at industrial speed. The
chapter's insight is that the departure is the mechanism, not a failure of it:
California's weak enforcement of non-competes and its dense geography make exit
cheap, and cheap exit is what compounds.

**The key fact.** Shockley located in Mountain View because his mother lived
there. The world's semiconductor industry sits on the San Francisco Peninsula in
part because a Nobel laureate wanted to be near his mother.

**The human anchor.** Shockley: co-inventor of the transistor, Nobel laureate,
catastrophic manager, and later a public advocate of eugenic argument — which
places him directly in the line that runs from Jordan in Act III ch. 3.

**Excluded voices.** Nobody, at this stage, and the chapter should say so
plainly. The semiconductor workforce is small, credentialed, and male. The
excluded arrive in the next decade, on the assembly lines and in the fabrication
plants, and the chapter should name that this is the calm before that.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the spinoff, not the invention, is the
Valley's reproductive mechanism by showing the industry's founding firms all
descend from one company's management failure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

William Shockley moved to Mountain View in 1956 because his mother lived there.
The world's semiconductor industry is located on the San Francisco Peninsula in
substantial part because a Nobel laureate wanted to be near his mother, and the
chapter opens on that contingency and lets it sit.

He had the standing to do it. He had co-invented the transistor, he had just won
the Nobel Prize, and the best young semiconductor physicists and engineers in
the country would move across the continent to work with him. He recruited an
extraordinary group.

He was also a catastrophic manager — paranoid, publicly ranking his staff,
publishing salaries, and at one point requiring lie detector tests over a
trivial workplace injury. Eight of his best engineers left in 1957, approached
Hayden, Stone, and were introduced to Arthur Rock, who found them a corporate
parent in Fairchild Camera and Instrument. Shockley called them traitors and the
name stuck.

The chapter's argument is that the departure is the mechanism rather than a
failure of it. The Valley reproduces by spinoff: talent exits bad leadership,
carries the knowledge out in its heads, and starts again a few miles away. What
makes that possible in California specifically is that non-compete agreements
are largely unenforceable there, that the geography is dense enough for a new
firm to recruit from an old one without anyone relocating, and that a form of
capital had just appeared which would fund people rather than assets.

There is almost nobody excluded at this stage, and the chapter says so plainly.
The semiconductor workforce in 1957 is small, credentialed, and male. The cost
arrives in the next decade, on the fabrication lines and in offshore assembly
plants, and the chapter names where it is coming.

Shockley's later career as a public advocate of eugenic argument places him
directly in the line running from David Starr Jordan in Act III — the same
claim, the same campus, a different discipline, fifty years apart.

Eight men walking out of a building is the founding event of the industry.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** He moved there because of his mother. Open on the contingency and
   let it sit.
2. **Shockley's standing in 1956.** The Nobel, the transistor, and why the best
   people in the field would move across the country for him.
3. **The recruitment.** Who he hired and from where. The concentration of talent
   is genuinely extraordinary and should be felt.
4. **The management collapse.** Paranoia, lie detector tests, published
   salaries, ranked lists. Specifics, sourced.
5. **The eight leave, 1957.** Named. The approach to Arthur Rock and Hayden,
   Stone; the search for a corporate parent; Fairchild Camera and Instrument.
6. **Why California made this possible.** Non-compete enforceability, geographic
   density, and the availability of capital that had not existed five years
   earlier.
7. **Shockley's later trajectory.** The eugenic advocacy. Connect explicitly to
   Jordan and Act III ch. 3 — the same argument, the same campus, a different
   discipline.
8. **The excluded, named as absent.** A small credentialed male workforce. Say
   that the cost arrives later and where.
9. **Landing.** Eight men leaving a building is the founding event of the
   industry. The spinoff is the mechanism, and Fairchild is about to demonstrate
   it at scale.

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
What happens when a genius cannot manage people?
:::

William Shockley located his semiconductor laboratory in Mountain View because
his mother lived there.

That is the reason. He had grown up in Palo Alto, his widowed mother was still
there, and when he decided in 1955 to leave Bell Laboratories and start a
company to commercialise the transistor, he put it in the town he came from.
Beckman Instruments financed it. Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory opened in
1956.

The world's semiconductor industry sits on the San Francisco Peninsula in
substantial part because of that decision, and it is worth letting the
contingency sit before explaining what made it stick.

## Why anyone came

Shockley in 1956 had standing that is hard to overstate.

He had co-invented the transistor at Bell Labs with John Bardeen and Walter
Brattain, and the three of them shared the Nobel Prize in Physics that year.
More to the point, his book *Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors* was the
field's standard text, and the junction transistor design that made commercial
devices practical was substantially his.

He was, in short, the most famous person in the most promising field in
electronics, and he was recruiting. He went after the best young physicists and
engineers he could identify, and he got them: people who had no particular
reason to move to a California town with no semiconductor industry, and who
moved because he asked.

The concentration of talent he assembled in one building in 1956 was
extraordinary, and there was nothing like it west of New Jersey.

## The management

He was also, by every surviving account, a catastrophic manager.

He posted salaries. He ranked his staff publicly. He required a lie detector
test after a minor workplace injury, on the theory that someone had sabotaged
the equipment. He recorded conversations. He telephoned people's former
colleagues to check their accounts of ordinary technical disagreements. He
changed the company's technical direction away from silicon transistors toward a
four-layer diode of his own design, over the objections of staff who thought the
transistor was where the market was, and they were right.

By the summer of 1957 a group of them had decided to leave.

## The eight

Eight men resigned in September 1957: Julius Blank, Victor Grinich, Jean Hoerni,
Eugene Kleiner, Jay Last, Gordon Moore, Robert Noyce, and Sheldon Roberts.
Shockley called them traitors, and the name stuck as the Traitorous Eight, which
is the sort of label a group only accepts if it rather likes it.

The mechanics of their departure are the important part, because they establish
a template.

They did not intend to found a company. They intended to move together to an
existing employer, and Eugene Kleiner's father's contact at the New York
investment bank Hayden, Stone was asked to help find one. The letter reached
Arthur Rock, a young banker there, who came out to California, met them, and
concluded that they should start a company rather than join one.

Rock then approached a long list of established firms — the number usually given
is around thirty — asking whether any would back a new semiconductor venture run
by eight men who had never managed anything. Almost all declined. Sherman
Fairchild's Fairchild Camera and Instrument agreed, with an option to buy the
whole company for a fixed sum if it succeeded.

Fairchild Semiconductor was incorporated in October 1957 in Mountain View.

## Why California made it possible

The chapter's structural argument is that the departure is the mechanism, not a
failure of it, and three features of the place made it repeatable.

The first is legal. California does not enforce non-compete agreements in
employment contracts, a position that goes back to the state's original civil
code in 1872 and has held ever since. An engineer in Massachusetts who left a
firm to found a competitor could expect litigation. An engineer in California
could not. Route 128 around Boston had comparable talent, comparable
universities, and comparable federal money in 1957, and it did not produce the
same fan-out — and the enforceability of non-competes is among the more
persuasive explanations for the difference.

The second is geographic. The Peninsula is dense. A new firm could recruit from
an old one without anyone changing schools or selling a house, which lowers the
personal cost of leaving to almost nothing.

The third is financial, and it barely existed yet. Rock's involvement in the
Fairchild financing is the beginning of a form of capital designed to fund
exactly this kind of departure, and chapter 5 is about what happened when it
industrialised.

## Nobody excluded, yet

The chapter should say plainly that at this stage there is almost no excluded
class, because saying so makes the later chapters land harder.

The semiconductor workforce in 1957 is small, credentialled, overwhelmingly
male, and very well paid. The eight men who left Shockley were physicists and
engineers with doctorates and options. Nothing about their situation involves
anyone bearing a cost on their behalf.

That changes within six years, when Fairchild opens an assembly operation in
Hong Kong, and it changes on the domestic fabrication lines at the same time,
where the workforce was substantially women doing precise repetitive work with
solvents and acids. The next chapter is where the ledger opens.

## Silicon

One technical decision from this period deserves recording, because the region
is named after it.

Transistors in the early 1950s were made from germanium, which is easier to work
and performs well at low temperatures. Shockley's laboratory was set up to make
silicon devices, and silicon is harder: it melts at a much higher temperature,
it is more difficult to purify, and the fabrication problems were unsolved.

Silicon's advantages are that it tolerates heat, which matters for military and
industrial applications, that it is abundant, and — decisively, though this was
not fully appreciated in 1956 — that its oxide is a stable insulator that can be
grown directly on the surface of the wafer. That property is what makes the
planar process of the next chapter possible, and it has no equivalent in
germanium.

Shockley chose the harder material and was right about it, which is worth saying
in a chapter otherwise concerned with his failures. His company did not
commercialise the advantage. The men who left did, and the material they were
working with gave the region a name that a trade journalist put into print in
1971.

## Shockley afterwards

His company never recovered from the 1957 departures and was sold, resold, and
eventually closed.

He became a professor of engineering at Stanford in 1963. From the mid-1960s he
devoted his public life to arguing that intelligence was substantially
hereditary, that it varied by race, and that the resulting differential
reproduction constituted a national crisis — a position he advanced in lectures,
in interviews, and in proposals for voluntary sterilisation incentives. He was
protested and disinvited and kept going, and he regarded this work as more
important than the transistor.

Place him next to David Starr Jordan from Act III chapter 3 and Lewis Terman
from chapter 6, and the line is unbroken: three Stanford figures, across seventy
years, in three different disciplines, arriving at the same claim that human
quality is heritable and should govern policy.

The transistor and the sorting argument came out of the same building on the
same campus. The industry has kept one and forgotten the other, which is itself
worth noticing.

Eight men walked out of Shockley's building in 1957. What they built is the
subject of the next chapter, and what it fragmented into is the industry.
